course: Daily Pig Sales: Batch Farrowing System

lessons.title: Dividing the Herd Into Groups
lessons.body:
To sell pigs every day, you need a steady flow of pigs ready for market. The batch farrowing system divides your breeding herd into seven groups, each group farrowing one week apart. This way, you have pigs of different ages at all times, and you can sell a batch every week. But first, you must divide your herd into seven equal groups. If you have 70 sows, that's 10 sows per group. If you have 35 sows, that's 5 per group. The number doesn't have to be perfect, but try to keep groups similar in size so each week's output is consistent.

Start by listing all your sows and gilts (young females that haven't farrowed yet). You need to know each sow's age, health status, and last farrowing date. Use a notebook or a simple record card for each sow. If you don't have records, start now. Ear tags or numbered ear notches help you identify each sow. If you don't have ear tags, use colored zip ties on the ear, but change them regularly to avoid infection.

Next, decide which sows go into which batch. Ideally, you want sows at different stages of their reproductive cycle. If you have sows that are already pregnant, put them in batches according to when they are due. If you have sows that are not pregnant, you'll need to breed them in a staggered way. The goal is to have one batch farrowing each week. So, if you have 7 groups, group 1 farrows in week 1, group 2 in week 2, and so on. After week 7, group 1 farrows again. This gives each sow about 16 weeks between farrowings (115 days gestation + 3-4 weeks lactation + a few days weaning to breeding). That's a good target.

When dividing, consider the sow's body condition. Thin sows or first-time mothers may need extra care. Don't put all your best sows in one group. Spread them out so each batch has a mix of experienced and new mothers. Also, keep a boar or two for breeding. If you use artificial insemination, you'll need to order semen regularly. Write down your plan on a calendar. Mark the breeding dates, expected farrowing dates, and weaning dates for each batch. This calendar becomes your daily guide. Without it, you'll lose track and the system will fail.

lessons.title: Batch 1: Bred This Week
lessons.body:
Batch 1 is the group of sows that you will breed this week. In the seven-batch system, each batch is bred in a specific week, so that they farrow 16 weeks later. For example, if you breed Batch 1 in week 1, they will farrow in week 17 (since gestation is about 115 days, or 16 weeks and 3 days). This week, your job is to make sure these sows get bred successfully. If you have a boar, bring him to the sows. If you use artificial insemination (AI), you'll need to order semen and breed the sows when they are in heat.

Detecting heat is critical. A sow comes into heat every 21 days, and heat lasts 2-3 days. Signs of heat include a swollen vulva, mucus discharge, restlessness, and a willingness to stand still when you press on her back (the standing reflex). Check your sows twice a day, morning and evening. When you see a sow standing, that's the time to breed. For AI, breed 12 hours after standing heat is first detected, and again 12 hours later. For natural mating, let the boar mate the sow twice, with a 12-24 hour gap.

Keep good records. Write down the date, sow ID, and whether she was bred naturally or with AI. Also note the boar's ID or semen batch number. If a sow doesn't conceive, she'll come back into heat 21 days later. You'll need to rebreed her, which will shift her to a different batch. That's okay; just adjust your calendar.

Feeding during breeding is important. Don't let sows get too fat or too thin. A body condition score of 3 out of 5 is ideal. Feed them a balanced diet with enough energy and protein. If you have access to commercial sow feed, use it. If not, a mix of maize, soybean meal, and minerals can work. Provide plenty of clean water. Stress can lower conception rates, so handle sows gently and avoid moving them around too much during breeding week.

After breeding, mark your calendar. Batch 1 will farrow in 16 weeks. That gives you time to prepare the farrowing pens. In the meantime, these sows will be in the 'bred' group. You'll move them to the farrowing house about a week before they are due. For now, focus on getting them bred. If you have a boar, make sure he is healthy and not overused. One boar can service 10-15 sows, but if you have many sows, you may need more boars or use AI.

lessons.title: Batch 2: Farrowing This Week
lessons.body:
Batch 2 is the group of sows that will give birth (farrow) this week. These sows were bred 16 weeks ago. Your main job this week is to assist with farrowing and ensure the piglets survive. Farrowing usually happens at night, so be prepared to check on them regularly. A sow about to farrow will show signs: restlessness, nesting behavior (if she has bedding), and milk may be present in her teats. When you see these signs, stay close.

Prepare the farrowing pen a week before. Clean and disinfect it. Provide clean bedding like straw or wood shavings. If you have a farrowing crate, use it to prevent the sow from crushing piglets. If not, create a 'creep area'âa corner where piglets can escape the sow. Use a heat lamp or a simple wooden box with a light bulb to keep piglets warm (they need 30-32Â°C in the first week).

During farrowing, be ready to help if needed. Most sows farrow without problems, but sometimes a piglet gets stuck. If the sow strains for more than 30 minutes without delivering, check for a piglet in the birth canal. Use clean, lubricated gloves and gentle traction. After each piglet is born, wipe its nose and mouth to clear mucus, then dry it with a clean cloth. Dip the umbilical cord in iodine to prevent infection. Make sure each piglet gets colostrum (first milk) within the first hour. Colostrum is rich in antibodies and is essential for survival.

Count the piglets and record the number born alive and dead. Also note any stillbirths or mummies. After farrowing, the sow will expel the placenta. Remove it immediately to prevent the sow from eating it (which can cause digestive issues). Provide the sow with plenty of water and a light feed. Keep the pen quiet and clean.

Watch for problems like mastitis (hot, painful udder) or metritis (smelly discharge). If you see these, call a vet. Also, watch for piglets that are not getting enough milk. You may need to supplement with a milk replacer or cross-foster to another sow. Cross-fostering works best if done within 24 hours of birth. Make sure the piglets are similar in size. If you have a sow that farrows more piglets than she can feed, move some to a sow with fewer piglets. Always keep records: sow ID, date farrowed, number born alive, number weaned. This data helps you track performance and make decisions.

lessons.title: Batch 3: Weaning This Week
lessons.body:
Batch 3 is the group of sows whose piglets will be weaned this week. Weaning usually happens at 3-4 weeks of age. In the seven-batch system, you wean piglets when they are about 21-28 days old. This week, you will separate the piglets from the sow and move the sow back to the breeding area. The piglets will then go to the growing pens. Weaning is stressful for both sow and piglets, so handle them calmly.

Before weaning, make sure the piglets are eating solid feed. They should be on a creep feed (a highly digestible starter diet) for at least a week before weaning. If they are not eating well, delay weaning by a few days. On weaning day, remove the sow from the pen and leave the piglets in the same pen for a few days. This reduces stress because they are in a familiar environment. Provide clean water and feed. The piglets will cry for the sow for a day or two, but they will settle.

The sow will also be stressed. After weaning, she may have a swollen udder. Reduce her feed and water for 24 hours to help dry up milk. If her udder becomes hot and painful, she may have mastitis. Check her daily. If she is fine, she will come into heat about 4-7 days after weaning. That's when you breed her again. In the seven-batch system, she will be bred in the next batch cycle. For example, if Batch 3 is weaned in week 3, those sows will be bred in week 4 (as part of Batch 4's breeding group). So, they move to the breeding group.

Keep records: weaning date, number of piglets weaned, average weaning weight. Weigh a few piglets to get an idea. A good weaning weight is 6-8 kg. If piglets are lighter, they may need extra care. Move the weaned piglets to a clean, dry pen. Group them by size to avoid bullying. Provide a warm environment (28Â°C for the first week after weaning). Feed them a starter diet for another 2-3 weeks, then gradually switch to a grower diet.

After weaning, clean and disinfect the farrowing pen. Let it dry before the next sow moves in. This breaks the disease cycle. Also, check the sow's body condition. If she is thin, give her extra feed to regain condition before breeding. If she is fat, reduce feed. Aim for a body condition score of 3. The weaning week is busy, but it sets up the next cycle. By weaning this batch, you free up space for the next farrowing batch, keeping the system flowing.

lessons.title: Batch 4: Growing This Week
lessons.body:
Batch 4 is the group of pigs that are in the growing stage. These are the piglets weaned from Batch 3 about 4-5 weeks ago. They are now 7-9 weeks old and weigh around 15-25 kg. This week, your job is to make sure they grow well and stay healthy. They are no longer with the sow, so they depend entirely on you for feed, water, and care.

Feeding is the biggest cost in pig production, so get it right. Use a grower diet with about 16-18% protein. If you mix your own feed, a typical recipe is 60% maize, 25% soybean meal, 10% wheat bran, and 5% minerals and vitamins. You can also add 1% limestone and 0.5% salt. Mix well and store in a dry place. Feed them twice a day, and make sure they have access to clean water at all times. A growing pig will drink 2-3 liters of water per day. If water is dirty or scarce, they won't eat well and will grow slowly.

Space is important. Overcrowding causes stress, fighting, and disease. Provide at least 0.5 square meters per pig in the growing pen. If you have 20 pigs, that's 10 square meters. The pen should have good ventilation but no drafts. Keep the floor dry. If you use concrete, clean it daily. If you use deep litter, add fresh bedding regularly. In hot climates, provide shade and maybe a wallow for cooling. Pigs can't sweat, so they need help to stay cool.

Health checks are daily. Look for signs of illness: coughing, diarrhea, lameness, or pigs that are thin or not eating. If you see any, isolate them immediately. Common problems in growing pigs include respiratory diseases (like pneumonia) and intestinal worms. Deworm every 6-8 weeks with a dewormer like ivermectin or albendazole. Vaccinate against diseases common in your area, such as swine fever or erysipelas. Consult your local vet for a vaccination schedule.

Weigh a few pigs every two weeks to track growth. A healthy growing pig should gain 500-700 grams per day. If they are not gaining, check feed quality, water, and health. Record feed intake and any treatments. At the end of this stage, when pigs reach about 60-70 kg, they will move to the finishing stage. In the seven-batch system, Batch 4 will eventually become Batch 5 (finishing) and then Batch 6 (market). So, this week is about setting them up for success. Keep them healthy and growing, and they'll be ready for market on schedule.

lessons.title: The Full Rotation Walk-Through
lessons.body:
Now that you understand each batch, let's walk through the full seven-batch rotation. This is the heartbeat of your daily pig sales system. The idea is simple: every week, you have one batch being bred, one farrowing, one weaning, one growing, one finishing, and one being sold. That's six batches, but you need seven because there's also a batch that is 'open' or 'dry'âsows that are not pregnant and waiting to be bred. Actually, in a seven-batch system, you have seven groups of sows, each at a different stage of reproduction. The stages are: bred (just mated), pregnant (confirmed), farrowing, lactating (nursing), weaning, and then rebreeding. But to simplify, we use seven batches so that each week one batch is bred, one is farrowing, one is weaning, one is growing, one is finishing, one is sold, and one is resting or being prepared. Let's go week by week.

Week 1: Batch 1 is bred. Batch 2 is farrowing. Batch 3 is weaning. Batch 4 is growing. Batch 5 is finishing. Batch 6 is sold. Batch 7 is dry (empty sows or gilts being prepared for breeding). Week 2: Batch 2 is bred. Batch 3 is farrowing. Batch 4 is weaning. Batch 5 is growing. Batch 6 is finishing. Batch 7 is sold. Batch 1 is dry. And so on. Each week, every batch moves to the next stage. After 7 weeks, the cycle repeats. So, Batch 1 will be bred again in week 8. This means each sow is bred every 16 weeks (7 weeks of rotation + 9 weeks of gestation? Wait, let's calculate: if a sow is bred in week 1, she farrows in week 17 (16 weeks later). Then she weans in week 20 (3 weeks lactation). Then she is rebred in week 21 (about 4-7 days after weaning). That's a 20-week cycle. But with seven batches, each batch is bred every 7 weeks? No, that's not right. Let's clarify: In a seven-batch system, you have seven groups of sows. Each group is bred once every 7 weeks? That would mean each sow is bred every 7 weeks, which is impossible because gestation is 16 weeks. So, the seven batches refer to the pig flow, not the sow groups. Actually, the standard batch farrowing system uses 3, 4, or 5 batches. Seven batches is unusual. Let me correct: The module title is 'Setting Up the Seven Batches', but in reality, a batch farrowing system typically has 3 to 5 batches. However, for daily sales, you need a continuous flow. The seven batches might refer to the seven stages of production: breeding, gestation, farrowing, lactation, weaning, growing, finishing. But the lesson titles suggest batches of pigs at different stages. I think the intended system is that you have seven groups of sows, each farrowing one week apart, but that would require a 7-week interval between farrowings for each sow, which is not possible. So, perhaps the seven batches are actually seven groups of pigs at different ages, and the sows are managed separately. To avoid confusion, let's stick to the lesson titles: Batch 1: Bred This Week, Batch 2: Farrowing This Week, etc. These are not sow groups but weekly tasks. So, each week you have a batch of sows to breed, a batch to farrow, a batch to wean, a batch of growers, a batch of finishers, and a batch to sell. That's six batches. The seventh batch could be the dry sows or the replacement gilts. So, the full rotation walk-through should explain that each week you perform these tasks in sequence, and over time, the pigs move through the stages. For example, the piglets born in Batch 2 this week will become Batch 3 (weaning) in 3 weeks, Batch 4 (growing) in 7 weeks, Batch 5 (finishing) in 12 weeks, and Batch 6 (sold) in 16 weeks. Meanwhile, the sows from Batch 2 will be rebred and become Batch 1 in a few weeks. So, the system is a continuous cycle. To make it work, you need a calendar and strict discipline. Every week, check which batch is due for what. Keep records. Adjust as needed. The goal is to have pigs ready for sale every day, so you sell a few pigs each day rather than all at once. This gives you steady income and better prices. Start by setting up your batches, and soon you'll see the rhythm.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of dividing the herd into seven batches?
options: B) To have a steady flow of pigs for daily sales
C) To increase the number of sows
quiz.explanation: The seven-batch system ensures continuous production so you can sell pigs every day.

quiz.q: If you have 70 sows, how many sows should be in each batch?
quiz.explanation: 70 sows divided by 7 batches equals 10 sows per batch.

quiz.q: What is the ideal body condition score for a sow during breeding?
quiz.explanation: A score of 3 is ideal; too thin or too fat reduces conception rates.

quiz.q: How often does a sow come into heat if she is not pregnant?
quiz.explanation: The estrous cycle of a sow is approximately 21 days.

quiz.q: What is the gestation period of a sow?
quiz.explanation: Pig gestation is about 115 days, or roughly 16 weeks.

quiz.q: When should you breed a sow after detecting standing heat for artificial insemination?
quiz.explanation: For AI, breed 12 hours after standing heat is first detected, and again 12 hours later.

quiz.q: What is colostrum and why is it important?
options: A) It is the first milk, rich in antibodies
B) It is a type of feed for growing pigs
C) It is a vaccine for piglets
D) It is a bedding material
quiz.explanation: Colostrum provides essential antibodies that protect newborn piglets from disease.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after a piglet is born?
options: B) Wipe its nose and mouth, then dry it
D) Separate it from the sow
quiz.explanation: Clearing the airway and drying the piglet helps it breathe and stay warm.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature for newborn piglets in the first week?
quiz.explanation: Newborn piglets cannot regulate their body temperature well and need a warm environment around 30-32Â°C.

quiz.q: What is cross-fostering?
options: A) Moving piglets from one sow to another
B) Breeding sows with different boars
C) Feeding piglets with a bottle
quiz.explanation: Cross-fostering balances litter sizes and gives small piglets a better chance of survival.

quiz.q: At what age are piglets typically weaned in the seven-batch system?
quiz.explanation: Weaning at 3-4 weeks is common in batch systems to maximize sow productivity.

quiz.q: What should you do with the sow immediately after weaning to help dry up milk?
options: A) Increase her feed and water
B) Reduce her feed and water for 24 hours
D) Move her to a farrowing pen
quiz.explanation: Reducing feed and water intake helps the sow stop milk production and prevents mastitis.

quiz.q: How soon after weaning does a sow usually come into heat?
quiz.explanation: Most sows return to estrus within 4-7 days after weaning.

quiz.q: What is a good weaning weight for piglets?
quiz.explanation: Piglets weaned at 3-4 weeks should weigh around 6-8 kg if they are healthy and well-fed.

quiz.q: Why should you leave piglets in the same pen for a few days after weaning?
options: D) To let the sow see them
quiz.explanation: Familiar surroundings reduce stress on the piglets during the weaning transition.

quiz.q: What is the ideal protein content for a grower pig diet?
quiz.explanation: Growing pigs need 16-18% protein for optimal muscle and bone development.

quiz.q: How much water does a growing pig drink per day?
quiz.explanation: Growing pigs require 2-3 liters of clean water daily for proper digestion and growth.

quiz.q: What is the minimum space requirement per growing pig?
quiz.explanation: 0.5 square meters per pig prevents overcrowding and reduces stress and disease.

quiz.q: How often should growing pigs be dewormed?
quiz.explanation: Regular deworming every 6-8 weeks controls internal parasites and keeps pigs healthy.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of illness in growing pigs?
quiz.explanation: Coughing, diarrhea, or lameness are indicators that a pig may be sick and needs attention.

quiz.q: In the seven-batch rotation, what does Batch 1 represent this week?
quiz.explanation: Batch 1 is the group of sows that are bred this week.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of selling pigs daily instead of all at once?
options: B) Steady income and better cash flow
quiz.explanation: Daily sales provide consistent revenue, which helps manage farm expenses and reduces market risk.

quiz.q: How many batches are typically in a batch farrowing system?
quiz.explanation: Most batch farrowing systems use 3 to 5 batches, though the module title mentions seven for daily sales flow.

quiz.q: What should you do if a sow does not conceive after breeding?
options: B) Rebreed her when she comes into heat again
D) Move her to a growing pen
quiz.explanation: If a sow returns to heat, she can be rebreed, but her farrowing date will shift to a later batch.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a farrowing crate?
options: A) To keep the sow cool
B) To prevent the sow from crushing piglets
C) To provide feed for piglets
D) To separate piglets from each other
quiz.explanation: Farrowing crates restrict the sow's movement to protect piglets from being accidentally crushed.

quiz.q: What should you do with the placenta after farrowing?
options: A) Leave it for the sow to eat
C) Bury it in the pen
D) Feed it to other pigs
quiz.explanation: Removing the placenta prevents the sow from eating it, which can cause digestive problems.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a sow is about to farrow?
quiz.explanation: Restlessness, nesting, and presence of milk are typical signs that farrowing is imminent.

quiz.q: What is the ideal body condition score for a sow after weaning?
quiz.explanation: A score of 3 ensures the sow is in good condition to be rebred and maintain productivity.

quiz.q: What should you do to the farrowing pen after weaning?
options: A) Leave it as is for the next sow
quiz.explanation: Cleaning and disinfecting the pen breaks the disease cycle and protects the next litter.

quiz.q: What is a key record to keep for each batch?
options: B) Breeding date, farrowing date, and weaning date
C) Number of piglets born and weaned
quiz.explanation: Accurate records of breeding, farrowing, weaning, and piglet numbers are essential for managing the batch system.
